h1: How to Make Your School Playground Safe and Child-Friendly

props.title: How to Make Your School Playground Safe and Child-Friendly
props.summaryText: Seven steps every school can follow, from zoning by age and choosing the right surface to supervision, shade and a simple maintenance routine.
props.author: priya-nair
props.imageAlt: Schoolchildren playing on a see-saw in a school playground

takeaways.text: Start by dividing the playground by age group: pre-primary, primary and older children need different equipment.
Put an impact-absorbing surface under everything children can fall from, across the whole safety zone.
Plan the layout so staff on duty can see the whole area from one point.
Stagger break times if too many children use one structure at once.
A five-minute daily check and a monthly hands-on check catch most problems before they cause injuries.

faq.q: How can I make my school playground safer?
faq.a: Zone the playground by age, use an impact-absorbing surface under all equipment, keep clear safety zones around swings and slide exits, place the area where staff can supervise it, add shade, put up simple rules, and inspect the equipment daily and monthly.

faq.q: What equipment is safe for pre-primary children?
faq.a: Low platforms, short slides around 3 ft, spring riders, small climbers with gentle steps, crawl tunnels, sand and water play and play panels. Avoid tall towers, fast spinners and equipment with large gaps or high rungs.

faq.q: How many teachers should supervise the playground at break time?
faq.a: It depends on the number and age of children and the shape of the area. The key is that the staff on duty can see every part of the play area, with more supervision for younger children and for busy structures such as slides and swings.

faq.q: What should a school playground safety policy include?
faq.a: Age groups allowed in each zone, supervision arrangements, playground rules, a daily and monthly inspection routine with a named person responsible, a procedure for closing damaged equipment, and first-aid and incident reporting.
